title: God's hand is a metaphor
hookLine: God's "hand" and "eye" are figures of speech
carry: god has no body; the hand means acting

cards: "For with a strong hand hath the LORD brought thee out of Egypt." That line is in the Torah, and it's written inside the tefillin some Jews bind on the arm and head. A strong hand.
For some readers, an image comes with it: an enormous arm reaching down out of the clouds. Maimonides spent real effort trying to take that picture down.
And a scholar who read him closely pushed back, not on the picture, but on how harshly to judge the people who kept it.

teach.b: The hand is a metaphor. First, the list.

In the opening laws of the Mishneh Torah, Maimonides gathers the Torah's bodily words for God: under God's feet, written with God's finger, the hand of the LORD, the eyes of the LORD, the ears of the LORD.
All of these, he says, are spoken according to what human minds can grasp. God has no body. Second, what each organ is doing.

In the Guide he explains the pattern: an eye stands for perceiving, an ear for hearing, a hand for acting. When the Psalm says, "The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous," it means God's care reaches them.
The strong hand that brought Israel out of Egypt means God's power at work.

teach.h: EACH PICTURE POINTS AT AN ACTION.
teach.b: The picture points at an action, not a limb. Third, the stakes.
In his Laws of Repentance, Maimonides lists someone who says God has a body or form among those who deny a core belief. Fourth, the pushback.

teach.h: THE RAAVAD DEFENDS THE PLAIN READER.
teach.b: Rabbi Abraham ben David, known as the Raavad, wrote short critical notes on the code. On this line he wrote, in effect: why call such a person that?

People greater and better than he followed this idea, because of what they read in the verses and in the midrash. The Raavad wasn't saying God has a body. He was defending the sincere reader who took the words plainly.
Printed editions carry his notes beside the code: the code, and a reader who argued with it, side by side.

how: Students of the Mishneh Torah read Maimonides' text together with the Raavad's printed glosses, weighing both. Some commentators on the Torah also explain bodily words for God as figures of speech.

games.q: what does “the hand is a metaphor” mean?
o: God's hand in scripture is a figure for God's acting
a hand-shaped charm hung by a door for good luck
the hand of a scribe copying a Torah scroll

games.q: the hand is a metaphor — tap the pairs.

s: the Raavad wrote that God has a body
he didn't. he defended people who took the verses plainly from being condemned.
Maimonides treats God having no body as a core belief
in his Laws of Repentance, saying God has a body is listed among denials of a core belief.
in Maimonides' reading, God's hand means a hand that can't be seen
it isn't a limb at all. the picture points at an action: God's power at work.

games.q: you're the Raavad, writing in the margin. Maimonides says anyone who thinks God has a body denies a core belief. what do you write?
o: greater and better people than he followed that idea, because of the verses.
God really does have a body.
games.why: the Raavad doesn't claim God has a body. he objects to condemning sincere readers who took the verses plainly.

practice: Bring to mind one verse with a bodily picture of God in it, the strong hand, the eyes toward the righteous, and hold the picture just as it is.

Then reread it the way Maimonides would, asking what action it points at, power, attention, listening, and say the verse again with that meaning in place of the limb. Notice whether it feels farther away, or closer.

wordCard.voice: The hand is a metaphor. Maimonides' teaching that God's hand, eyes and ears in scripture are figures for God's acting, caring and hearing, since God has no body. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: hand. used for God's power and action in phrases like 'a strong hand'.

carryVoice: Your line: god has no body; the hand means acting. The strong hand points past itself, to God's power and care. I'll be here tomorrow.
